unit.title: Chemical Bonding and Structure of Materials
unit.blurb: Why atoms bond, covalent bonds and molecules, ions and ionic bonds, and how simple, giant covalent and ionic structures decide a substance's properties.

O1.t: Explain that atoms bond to reach a full, stable outer shell.

O2.t: Describe a covalent bond as a shared pair of electrons and draw dot-and-cross diagrams of simple molecules.

O3.t: Describe how ions form and explain an ionic bond as electrostatic attraction.

O4.t: Relate simple molecular, giant covalent and giant ionic structures to their properties.

captions: Welcome to Atomic Education.
This lesson was written by the Atomic teaching team to
help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence.
Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 5: Chemical Bonding and Structure of Materials.
Diamond and coal are both made of carbon,
yet one sparkles and the other is dull and crumbly.
The secret is chemical bonding: how atoms are joined changes how materials behave.
Electrons orbit the nucleus in shells, or energy levels.
The outer shell matters most.
Group 18 atoms, like neon, have a full outer shell of 8 electrons:
a stable electronic configuration.
That's why they hardly react.
Other atoms, like sodium with one outer electron or chlorine with seven,
are not stable, so they react.
To reach a full outer shell, atoms form chemical bonds.
They can share outer electrons, making covalent bonds, or lose or gain electrons,
making ionic bonds.

captions: In a covalent bond, two non-metal atoms share a pair of electrons,
forming a molecule. Two hydrogen atoms share their electrons so both get a full shell.
Dot-and-cross diagrams show one atom's electrons as dots, the other's as crosses.
An oxygen atom has 6 outer electrons and needs 2 more.
It shares one pair with each of two hydrogen atoms,
making a water molecule with two covalent bonds.
Hydrogen chloride has one covalent bond.
Methane has four, because carbon has four outer electrons to share.
That's why carbon forms so many different molecules.
Many substances we meet every day are made of small covalent molecules.
Here are four.
Every water molecule has an oxygen atom sharing a
pair of electrons with each of two hydrogen atoms.
The bubbles in fizzy drinks are carbon dioxide:
a carbon atom joined to two oxygen atoms by covalent bonds.
Natural gas for cooking is mostly methane.
Carbon shares its four outer electrons with four hydrogen atoms.
The oxygen we breathe is made of O₂ molecules,
where two oxygen atoms share two pairs of electrons.
These small molecules are all gases or liquids at room temperature,
because the forces between the molecules are weak.
Pause and think of one more covalent substance.

captions: An atom that loses or gains electrons becomes a charged ion.
Metals lose electrons to form positive ions, or cations: sodium loses one.
Non-metals gain electrons to form negative ions, or anions: chlorine gains one.
Opposite charges attract. This electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions is an ionic bond,
forming sodium chloride: table salt.
Magnesium loses two electrons,
so it bonds with two chloride ions to make magnesium chloride.

captions: Electrodes connected to a bulb are dipped into solid salt crystals,
a salt solution, and a sugar solution.
Predict: in which will the bulb light?
Pause and decide.
Watch. The circuit is completed in each beaker in turn.
Only the salt solution lights the bulb.
Solid salt and the sugar solution do not.
Explain what you saw.
Salt is an ionic compound.
In the solid, its ions are fixed in a lattice and cannot move.
Dissolved in water, the ions are free to move and carry charge,
so the solution conducts.
Sugar is made of covalent molecules with no charge,
so its solution does not conduct.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
Substances made of small, separate molecules, like bromine, oxygen, carbon dioxide and water,
have a simple molecular structure.
They have low melting and boiling points and don't conduct electricity.
Bromine boils at just 59 degrees Celsius.
In giant covalent structures, atoms form a huge network of bonds.
In diamond, each carbon bonds to four others, so it's extremely hard.
In graphite, each bonds to three, in sliding layers,
so it's soft and conducts electricity.
Ionic compounds like sodium chloride form a giant ionic lattice held by strong electrostatic forces,
so they have high melting points.
They conduct electricity only when melted or dissolved,
because then the ions can move.
Here are the melting points of four solids, from published chemistry data.

adv.frame: Both are … In diamond … so … In graphite … so … Graphite conducts because …

rubric.pt: Both are giant structures with strong covalent bonds
In diamond each carbon atom is bonded to four others
This rigid structure makes diamond hard
In graphite each carbon atom is bonded to three others, in layers
Weak forces between layers let them slide, so graphite is soft
Graphite has free electrons that can move and carry charge; diamond has none

adv.model: Diamond and graphite are both giant structures in which carbon atoms are joined by strong covalent bonds. In diamond, each carbon atom is bonded to four others. This makes a rigid structure in every direction, so diamond is very hard. In graphite, each carbon atom is bonded to only three others, forming flat layers. There are only weak forces between the layers, so they slide over each other and graphite is soft. Each carbon atom in graphite has one free electron that can move, so graphite conducts electricity, but diamond has no free electrons.

adv.prompt: * Advanced. PubChem gives the melting point of magnesium oxide as 2852 °C, much higher than sodium chloride (801 °C), though both are giant ionic lattices. Suggest why, and give one use that depends on this property.

rubric.pt: magnesium oxide has ions with larger charges (Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ v Na⁺ and Cl⁻)
so the attraction / ionic bonds are much stronger, needing more energy to break

adv.model: Magnesium oxide is made of Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions, which have double the charges of Na⁺ and Cl⁻. The attraction between them is much stronger, so far more energy is needed to break up the lattice. Because it does not melt even at very high temperatures, it is used to line furnaces and kilns.
